kp.k: Employer forecasts have defined coverage and methodological limits
kp.d: The World Economic Forum reports 1,043 unique company responses representing more than 14.1 million employees across 22 industry clusters and 55 economies. Its sampling targets significant national and multinational employers, with a threshold of 500 employees; small enterprises and informal-sector employment are outside scope. Employment projections combine employer expectations with ILO occupational data, covering 1.18 billion employees rather than the entire global workforce. Missing Chinese occupational data are addressed using a multiplier that assumes China's occupational structure follows global patterns. These are forecast structural changes, not observed displacement or ordinary employee turnover.

kp.k: GenAI substitution estimates rely on model self-assessment
kp.d: Indeed's contribution assesses more than 2,800 granular skills using GPT-4o's assessment of its own theoretical knowledge, problem-solving capability and need for physical action, using an August 2024 skills database. No assessed skill receives the highest substitution rating; 69% fall into low or very-low capacity categories, and 28.5% into moderate capacity. The report highlights limitations for physical work, nuanced judgement and human interaction, while finding greater potential in digitally mediated knowledge tasks. These estimates are model-based skill assessments, not observed job losses or independent demonstrations of task competence.

pts.k: The World Economic Forum reports employer expectations of simultaneous AI-driven job creation, displacement, business transformation and skill change, including declining demand for legal secretaries.
pts.d: This is principally a cross-domain labour-market report. WEF reports that 86% of surveyed employers expect AI and information processing technologies to transform their businesses by 2030. Its extrapolations attribute approximately 11 million jobs created and 9 million displaced to this technology category, with Figure 2.6 showing a net gain of 1.8 million. These are projections, not observed employment changes, and the category is broader than generative AI. Separately, the report projects 170 million jobs created and 92 million displaced across all studied macrotrends; these totals are not AI-only effects. Legal Secretaries and Legal Officials appear among the 15 fastest-declining roles in Figure 2.2. WEF interprets the appearance of legal secretaries and graphic designers just outside the top 10 as a possible indication of GenAI's increasing capacity for knowledge work, attributing their decline to AI and information processing and broadening digital access. It does not predict the disappearance of lawyers: the economy profiles give a global net growth projection of 2% for Lawyers. Across employers, AI-response strategies include upskilling existing staff (77%), hiring AI-tool development talent (69%), hiring people able to work alongside AI (62%), reorienting business opportunities (49%), redeploying workers from affected jobs (47%) and downsizing where AI can replicate work (41%). WEF also anticipates a shift from predominantly human task delivery toward automation and collaboration, rather than a uniform replacement of people.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The main evidence is an employer expectations survey and extrapolation using ILO employment data; supplementary evidence includes workplace studies, platform data and GPT-4o skill assessments.
pts.d: The methodology reports 1,043 unique company responses, representing more than 14.1 million employees across 22 industry clusters and 55 economies. WEF combines respondents' occupational growth and decline expectations with ILO employment statistics and maps its modified O*NET occupational taxonomy to ISCO. The resulting job projections cover approximately 1.18 billion employees in occupations with sufficient survey data. Attribution of job changes to individual trends comes from respondents, rather than causal measurement of AI's employment effects. The methodology applies caps to trend–occupation effects, excludes attribution pairs with fewer than three votes, and uses a multiplier for China under an assumption that its occupational structure follows global patterns. WEF supplements the survey with cited workplace research by Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond; Noy and Zhang; and Dell’Acqua and colleagues, describing productivity benefits and capability-dependent risks without reproducing numerical effects here. The Indeed collaboration assesses more than 2,800 granular skills using GPT-4o's assessment of its own knowledge, problem-solving and physical-task capabilities, based on August 2024 data. It classifies 69% as having low or very low substitution capacity, 28.5% as moderate, and none as very high. This is a model-based assessment of skills, not demonstrated replacement of entire jobs or a legal-work benchmark. Coursera training enrolments and LinkedIn AI job and skill concentration provide additional indicators of adoption and demand.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Employment and workforce forecasts concern 2025–2030, while productivity and substitution claims are conditional on capabilities, deployment choices and training.
pts.d: The report was published in January 2025 and principally forecasts the following five years. Its methodological account dates survey collection to May–September 2024, although other passages describe late-2024 collection or May–August. WEF presents employment estimates as conditional on current predictions, not inevitable outcomes. It says long-term productivity gains remain uncertain and that workplace benefits depend on using GenAI within its capabilities; stretching beyond those capabilities can produce adverse results. Broader expert-task access and more efficient professional problem-solving are presented as possibilities advanced by cited observers, not established findings. WEF argues that genuine improvements in output are more likely when development complements human capabilities, whereas incentives and policy choices favouring substitution could increase inequality and unemployment. The Indeed analysis concerns the current generation of GenAI, with limitations involving physical execution, nuanced judgement and human interaction; future integration with robotics could alter that assessment. Task-share projections do not measure changes in absolute output or establish equivalent headcount reductions. Small enterprises and informal-sector employment are outside the survey's intended scope, limiting transfer to the entire legal market.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Effects differ across occupations, industries, organizational sizes and economies; legal support roles face a different forecast from lawyers.
pts.d: The direct legal-related claim concerns projected decline in legal secretarial work, alongside a modest global growth forecast for lawyers. Country profiles show differing lawyer projections, including Canada (+3%), Colombia (-1%), Hong Kong SAR, China (+8%), Kazakhstan (-5%), Lithuania (-3%), Nigeria (+5%) and Uzbekistan (+11%); these are all-trend employer forecasts, not isolated AI effects. Professional Services is a broad sector, not a law-firm-only sample. Its profile projects predominantly human task delivery falling from 52% to 31%, collaborative delivery rising from 30% to 37%, and technology-led delivery rising from 18% to 32% by 2030. Within that sector, 83% plan AI-related reskilling, 78% plan to hire AI-tool development talent and 63% plan to hire people able to work alongside AI. Across the economy, newer or average-performing workers may benefit from AI supplying tacit knowledge, while less-specialized workers could undertake more expert tasks and skilled professionals could solve problems more efficiently. Adoption is described as uneven: information technology leads construction, low-income economies lag richer economies, and larger employers more often anticipate AI-driven transformation. WEF identifies potential risks to workers whose roles are automated or who cannot obtain training, and raises the distributional question of whether workers will share in greater output and income generated by machines and algorithms. These findings do not separately establish effects on law-firm partnerships, legal pricing, legal-service clients or access to justice.
